projectOutComesReport:
Deformation on the surface of Earth, including faulting responsible for earthquakes, is produced by the motion of tectonic plates. It is widely accepted that thermal convection in the mantle drives plate motion, but details of that convection and how exactly it moves the plates are poorly understood. Oceanic plates make up 70% of the Earth's surface and offer important windows into mantle convection, yet they are largely unexplored due to the lack of seismic data from the ocean basins. Questions abound regarding the thermal structure of oceanic plates, the significance of volcanism in the middle of oceanic plates, and how the convecting mantle beneath the plates controls their movements. Undulations in the gravity field and un-explained shallowing of the ocean floors hint at small-scale thermal convection beneath the oceanic plates. This project exploits community advances in ocean-bottom seismographs to provide unprecedented new constraints on the nature of mantle convection beneath remote, previously unexplored regions of the Pacific plate.

Intellectual Merit.  We collected ~12 months of broadband ocean-bottom seismograph (OBS) data in two 30-station arrays deployed at two distinct plate ages (~30 Ma and ~90 Ma) in the central and south Pacific. Using earthquakes and ambient seismic signals recorded on these arrays, we provide unique new constraints on the dynamics of the oceanic lithosphere-asthenosphere system.  Three-dimensional images of seismic wavespeed in the asthenosphere beneath both arrays show clear evidence of distinctive high and low velocity variations, which we interpret as small-scale thermal convection organized into linear roll-like structures by shearing from the overriding plate.  The imaged convection can explain the linear corrugations in the gravity field, provides a potential mechanism for intra-plate volcanism, and likely can explain the flattening of the age versus depth curve in old ocean plates.  On average, the asthenosphere beneath both regions appears to be anomalously weak; estimates of surface-wave velocity and amplitude decay across the arrays require distinctive low velocity, high-attenuation channels beneath the plate in both regions, suggesting mantle viscosities that are approximately 10 times weaker than those found in a comparable region in the north central Pacific.  Finally, a strong directional dependence (anisotropy) of surface-wave velocity is observed across both arrays, which we interpret in the context of strong depth variations in crystallographic deformation fabric in the olivine-rich mantle rocks in both the lithosphere and asthenosphere.  Fabric strength in the lithosphere is generally quite strong, suggesting that seafloor spreading represents the dominant form of coherent deformation the oceanic mantle.  The older array appears to be an exception to this general observation, with weak fabric strength at an unusual orientation that implies significant complexity in the seafloor spreading process when the seafloor in this region was formed.  In the asthenosphere beneath both regions, the fabric strength and direction variations indicate that mantle deformation consists of a combination of buoyancy and/or pressure-induced flow modulated by shearing from the overriding plate.  Beneath the older array, the rock fabric direction changes abruptly at ~75 km depth, marking a sharp transition from the lithosphere to the asthenosphere that may suggest a compositional rheological change from a dry (strong) plate to a damp (weaker) underlying mantle.      

Broader Impacts.  OBS data remain a rare and valuable resource, and this project generated two high-quality datasets that are openly available to scientists worldwide through the NSF-supported seismic data archive. Additional geophysical data collected during the seagoing research expeditions (multibeam bathymetry, gravity) have also been archived in NSF-supported marine geophysics repositories for community use.  The project provided the primary support, important data, and training opportunities for two PhD students and an early-career (Post-Doctoral) scientist, as well as support and research experience for several undergraduate students; additional students and Post-Docs were supported at partner institutions.  Through an Apply-to-Sail program, we provided experience doing research at sea for the next generation of scientists.  Over the course of the four seagoing expeditions, we supported the participation of 30 early career scientists, from undergraduate to junior faculty level.  All participants received training in OBS instrumentation, seagoing deck operations, and processing of multibeam bathymetry data.  Three early-career scientists gained experience serving as chief and/or co-chief scientists on seagoing expeditions.  The scientific results of this project have significant implications far beyond marine geophysics, especially in the fields of geodynamics and mineral physics.  Our new observations and associated interpretations summarized above provide unique constraints on the viscosity of the asthenosphere, the nature of small-scale buoyancy driven and larger-scale pressure-driven flow, the dominant deformation mechanisms in the mantle, and the impact of these processes on surface deformation and the tectonic plates.

abstractText:
Developing computer models of cardiovascular disease growth requires an organ-scale model of blood flow, a cell-scale model of cell biology, and a framework to couple these models. Such computer models could help predict cardiovascular disease by simulating spatial and temporal patterns of disease growth. To develop these models, we need a software infrastructure that integrates modeling techniques from multiple disciplines. This project will develop software for this purpose and will apply the software to the calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD) problem, which is prevalent in aging adults. The project will also help to understand the interaction between the fundamental biological and mechanical processes involved in CAVD. The project leverages existing resources at Northern Arizona University to perform outreach activities targeting underrepresented minority students in the region. The outcome of this study will contribute to advancing the national health and improving our scientific understanding of the interaction between different processes in cardiovascular disease. 

During the past two decades, significant advances have been made in the development of organ-scale patient-specific computational models of cardiovascular disease. These models often focus on a specific spatial and temporal scale and their goal is to quantify biomechanical biomarkers of cardiovascular disease growth. However, quantitative information about disease growth over long time scales is missing in these models. The goal of this project is to 1) Develop a software platform for multiscale two-way coupling between organ-scale biomechanics and cell-scale systems biology models. 2) Apply the computational framework to study the long-term spatial and temporal progression of CAVD. The organ-scale model will be based on continuum solid and fluid mechanics models, and the cell-scale model will be based on systems of differential equations. The developed software infrastructure could be applied to patient-specific data to model disease progression patterns. This will enable the development of transformative models that advance our knowledge of cardiovascular disease. The project will train highly interdisciplinary researchers at the interface of software development, biomechanics, and biology. Outreach activities will promote STEM participation by demonstrating the beauty of computer science and engineering blended and applied to biomedical applications.

abstractText:
Nontechnical Description: 
During the CoVid-19 pandemic, one of the most challenging aspects is the lack of testing to detect and trace infections and implementing a strategy to carefully re-open the country and economic activity. The lack of testing has resulted in uncertainties about public health policies. Testing is necessary not only for diagnosis but also for tracking to control the pandemic. This work is based on non-traditional techniques for the detection of virus in infected patients. The project will develop an alternative method based on the advances of physics and understanding of the quantum mechanical aspects of interaction of light with matter. The technique will be based on recent discoveries in nanotechnology and solid-state physics, allowing the development of spectroscopy techniques to detect the SARs-Cov-2 virus. The method, named Single Molecule Surface Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (SM-SERS), If successful, will allow a fast, inexpensive, and much more precise and reliable method to detect infections. The method is based on the detection the S proteins of the virus, which participate in the cell infection. The ability of SM-SERS to detect down to one molecule of protein will allow early detection of infection and follow up of patients who recover from the illness. In addition, further analysis of the SM-SERS data will help to understand changes on the virus proteins and can help in the development of antiviral drugs.

Technical Description:
During the CoVid-19 pandemic, one of the most challenging aspects has been the lack of testing to detect and trace infections. The limitations in quantities and quality of test kits have resulted in uncertainties about public health policies. Testing is necessary not only for diagnosis but also for tracking to control the pandemic. The practical difficulties to increase the number of available test kits involve, among other things, difficulty in production of the chemicals needed for the test. The most used test, technically known as RT-qPCR, is costly, has a long turnaround time and, although it is highly sensitive, produces many false negatives and are based on biochemical methods. This work is based on the Raman spectroscopy in its SM-SERS modality. The method is based on amplification of the inelastically scattered light by localized surface plasmons on metal nanoparticles. The main goal will be to establish a Raman signature of the spike glycoprotein of the SARS-CoV-2 virus that can be used to develop a detection test. Previous research in the PI's group indicates that tests based on analysis of sialylated glycoproteins have high sensitivity, specificity, and low percentage of false negatives. The project will develop a new type of plasmonic nanoparticles combined with ionic liquids that will improve the nanoparticle delivery to solutions containing the virus. A second interest will be to study the fine peak structure, which is related to morphological changes in the proteins. This will be useful for development of antiviral drugs and the basic understanding of the biology of the virus.

This Rapid Response Research (RAPID) grant supports research that will develop a new method for viral testing with funding from the CARES Act managed by the Condensed Matter Physics Program in the Division of Materials Research of the Mathematical and Physical Sciences Directorate.

projectOutComesReport:
In the last two years the wold has been shaken by the worst health  pandemic in a century. The emergence of the SARS-CoVi-2 virus demanded a broader response from scientists which were not directly involved in health related research .When the NSF  invited  scientists in areas of Physics of Materials to perform  research related to the pandemic , an interdisciplinary group was formed at the Northern Arizona University to apply techniques normally used in Physics research to study the SARS-CoVi-2 virus. We combined expertize on nanotechnology ,virology ,materials synthesis   and machine learning methods to develop a new technique to detect the virus using Surface Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (SERS). We used silver nanowires and gold nanostars to enhance the signal from the virus and achieved a sensitivity down to a single virion particle .We demonstrated that this method allows the detection of the virus on saliva in minutes .However we further develop the technique as a tool  to characterize the virus proteins .We found out that we can distingush between variants this is beyond what rapid testing methods can do .We have also found that we can learn about details of the viral proteins structure which can help to develop vaccines and antiviral medications..

The SERS technique is now being developed on a rapid test that can not only sort out viral variants but can also detect very early stages of infection which very high sensitivity  .this technique can in the future be extended to other viral and bacterial infections .We have also now a tool to complement other methods to study viral structure and advance our capabilities of fighting the present  and future outbreaks.

abstractText:
SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, has become a global epidemic, spreading rapidly through communities across our country and around the globe. Accurate forecasting of disease spread is a critical tool for effectively planning outbreak responses, allowing us to predict how many people will be infected, how many patients will be in hospitals at any given time, and the resource needs (e.g. ventilators) at each hospital. Most modeling studies of SARS-CoV-2 have so far focused on predicting how the virus will spread in densely populated cities like New York City, but the virus is also rapidly spreading in more sparsely populated, rural regions.  To accurately model outbreak dynamics in more rural areas, more realistic mathematical models are needed that can represent mid-sized population centers separated by large areas of low population density. This project will develop and refine these more advanced mathematical models to understand how population density and interconnectedness influence the trajectory of epidemic outbreaks. Importantly, the project will deploy model projections in near-real-time to aid in local public health interventions, via a secure web portal accessible to local and regional response planners. Model output will also be linked to the resources available at specific local and regional hospitals in a broad rural area, so that these hospitals can better manage the impacts of the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic. The modeling system and web application will serve as a framework for rapidly responding to future outbreaks. 

Most epidemiological models that have been developed to forecast the spread of SARS-CoV-2 make assumptions that are likely only realistic in dense urban centers, such as frequency-dependent transmission dynamics, a lack of stochastic processes, and a lack of density-dependent effects. In this project, models will be developed that are more appropriate for sparse metapopulations, accounting for multiple sources of stochasticity, population movement across a landscape, density-dependent transmission, and spatial heterogeneity in transmission rates. The project will use advanced statistical computing algorithms to fit the models to data from a large rural region. This fitting routine will identify the most appropriate transmission functions that describe longitudinal patterns of case-counts and will allow the project to release data-informed predictions of SARS-CoV-2 spread in near-real-time. These model forecasts will be developed in collaboration with public health experts and healthcare practitioners to respond to the needs of under-served, rural communities. The secure web application will provide predictions of hospitalization rates at fine spatial grains so that already strained, rural hospital systems can adapt and plan under different intervention scenarios.

jrnl.artTitl: A sliding window approach to optimize the time-varying parameters of a spatially-explicit and stochastic model of COVID-19
jrnl.auth: Ratnavale S and Hepp C and Doerry E and Mihaljevic J

program: RAPID, COVID-19 Research
projectOutComesReport:
The use of epidemiological models has a long history in responses to infectious disease outbreaks, but forecasts from these models are typically made at larger spatial scales, such as entire states, which often ignore variation in population structure and behavior at smaller spatial scales can influence disease dynamics.  Model forecasts of disease made at large spatial scales usually have limited utility in informing public health interventions at the neighborhood, community, or county level relevant in an actual pandemic, as vividly demonstrated during the recent SARS-COV-2 pandemic.  Our approach uses spatial disease modeling to capture important, fine-scale heterogeneities in populations across space that affect how diseases spread, so that we can make more reliable, smaller-scale forecasts of disease.

During the first two years of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, our team developed software tools and modeling methods to put spatial epidemiological modeling technologies in the hands of state and county officials in Arizona. Our developments are general enough to be applied to many epidemiological contexts, such that the results of our project should better prepare our nation for future pandemic threats.

We first developed an advanced epidemiological model to make forecasts of COVID-19 hospitalizations at the scale of individual counties within Arizona. To improve predictions, our model was built to reflect heterogeneities in sub-populations within each county, such as accounting for rural versus urban population structures. To disseminate our modeling techniques, we created an open-source software package, SPARSEMODr, which allows users to create custom simulations of our COVID-19 model. Our package allows users to better understand how non-pharmaceutical public health interventions can influence transmission of SARS-CoV-2 throughout an epidemic. SPARSEMODr also allows users to create their own spatial arrangement of populations and simulate cases in which transmission rates vary spatially, due to, for instance, variations in human behavior or mobility, or in response to hypothetical public health interventions (lockdowns, masking, etc.). We created several vignettes that demonstrate how to use our software package in a variety of contexts; SPARSEMODr should be useful for educating the next generation of modelers on important disease dynamics that shaped the early COVID-19 pandemic.

Our team worked closely with state and county officials to generate and disseminate custom modeling reports during the first two years of the pandemic. Specifically, we created a cyberinfrastructure and automated report-generation pipeline to (a) process and ingest state-level disease surveillance data (updated daily) for all Arizona counties; (b) model disease propagation dynamics for each of the 15 Arizona counties to create customized 30-day projections; and (c) generate customized, easy-to-read, standardized reports for local county health officials, including summary visualizations of past-present-predicted disease progress under best-average-worst case scenarios and ?expert digests? to highlight relevant features in the data.  

Our team created a secure web portal to provide controlled, authenticated access to designated state and county public health officials. Our cyberinfrastructure and automated report-generation pipeline provides a model for efficient, automated communication of the results of sophisticated epidemiological modeling to diverse stakeholders and how to actively engage with local public health experts.

Our team also made technical advances in the statistical fitting of these complex, spatial models to geo-referenced data. To make accurate forecasts of disease spread, spatial models need to have maximally accurate estimates of disease transmission rates within individual local populations, which can vary over time due to changes in population behavior or public health interventions that are implemented to slow the spread of pathogens. Transmission rates can be estimated computationally based on evolving disease surveillance data, but this is both complicated and arduous to do for many distinct local (sub)populations.  We developed a novel and efficient statistical algorithm to estimate time-varying transmission rates applicable to any modeling effort that represents spatial heterogeneity across geographic space, i.e., useful for any spatial modeling effort. Briefly, our method estimates time-varying transmission rates across space using time slices of county-level data on new hospitalizations observed per day. To address the enormous computational complexity involved, we developed implementation methods that leverage a high-performance computing environment to run thousands of grid searches concurrently to scour a large parameter space. We used simulated data to verify that our method performs very well in hypothetical urban, sub-urban, and rural type counties. This model-fitting routine could easily be generalized to many epidemiological modeling frameworks (i.e., not just for SARS-CoV-2), offering a flexible and efficient method to estimate time-varying parameters from geo-referenced data sets.

During our project, we also provided training and professional development opportunities for an undergraduate student in computer science, a professional systems programmer, a Master?s student in informatics, and a postdoctoral researcher.

abstractText:
This project aims to understand how crust is formed in volcanic arcs above subduction zones.  Crustal formation within volcanic arcs is a profoundly important process that continually replenishes the mass of the continents, whose constant weathering and erosion provide the source of elemental nutrients that drive Earth's biogeochemical cycles.  Remarkably, the creation of new continental material and the recycling of material back into the mantle have remained balanced on Earth over hundreds of millions of years. Understanding this balance is key to understanding the habitability of the planet. All of Earth's crust is created from partial melts of the deeper mantle that rise upward and then freeze to form the crust.  The building blocks of continental crust form when water released from a subducting tectonic plate lowers the melting temperature of the mantle, creating magma that rises and accumulates in volcanic arcs.  The process of arc-crust formation has been the focus of many studies, but our understanding of these process is far from a complete.  Questions persist because arc processes are complex and episodic, they occur over a range of spatial scales and depend on variables such as the age of the subducting plate and the evolutionary stage of a given arc, which may never reach a steady state.  The study location of this project is the Andreanof segment of the Aleutian arc.  Coincidentally, this location coincides with the epicenter of the 1957 Great Aleutian earthquake, the third largest earthquake of the last century and with the largest aftershock zone of any earthquake ever recorded.  Active-source seismic techniques will be used to image the seismic velocity structure of the entire crust along and across this arc segment to address many of the unanswered questions of arc-crust formation.  These same methodologies can be used to address questions related to earthquake and volcanic hazards common to volcanic arcs.  The education component of this project will train a cohort of the next generation of scientists in the acquisition and advance analyses of these types of data.

Through this grant an active-source seismic experiment will be conducted in the Andreanof segment of the Aleutian arc in order to study arc-crust formation processes.  Many basic questions about arc-crust formation processes remain, including the source and variability of primary arc magmas, where and how these magmas fractionate to produce the characteristic arc geochemical signatures of crustal rocks, the role of water in all of these processes, the bulk composition of arc crust and its basic architecture and similarity to continental crust, the forcing functions for all of these processes and the temporal and spatial variability of those forcings, and the mass balance of the entire system.  Substantial advance can be made by focused, multi-disciplinary study of an arc segment that has simple, well known magmatic and tectonic histories, well studied geochemistry, and sufficient along-strike variability to capture many of the processes that are believed to control arc-crust geochemical and structural evolution.  The Andreanof segment is one of very few locations that satisfy these criteria. It consists of an intact, arc massif formed during three identifiable and dated magmatic episodes; it is only modestly deformed and exhibits along-strike variability in active volcanism from primarily basaltic in the east to andesitic/dacitic in the west.  The seismic experiment supported by this grant will consist of one transect along the entire length of the segment and two arc-crossing transects.  Multi-channel seismic (MCS) data, recorded on an 8-km-long streamer, and ocean-bottom seismic data, with instrument spacings of 10 to 15 km, will be acquired along each transect, and these data will be analyzed with advanced tomographic and MCS imaging methodologies to produce seismic velocity and reflectivity images that will reveal, for the first time, the full crustal architecture of an intact arc massif at a segment scale.  These images will provide estimates of composition that will inform models of melt emplacement and fractionation, and enable a number of specific questions to be addressed, including: What is the bulk composition, thickness and basic architecture of oceanic-arc crust, How are variations in factors such as primary magma composition and crustal processing of magmas expressed in bulk arc crustal composition and structure, and What is the fate of mafic/ultra-mafic cumulates?
